title: Aristotle's Politics
orientation: This chapter surveys Aristotle's Politics: his account of the State's natural origin and purpose, his defense of slavery and critique of trade and usury, his sixfold classification of constitutions, his analysis of revolution and tyranny, and his proposals about the ideal State's size, citizenship, and education. Russell treats it as historically important -- a major source of ideas that shaped political thought through the Middle Ages -- while repeatedly noting how thoroughly it reflects the 'common prejudices of educated Greeks' of Aristotle's own time, and how startlingly, at points (notably the anatomy of tyranny), it anticipates twentieth-century dictatorship.
historical_background: Russell stresses that the Politics is entirely concerned with the Greek City State and shows no awareness of the transformation Alexander was already effecting in the world -- 'there is no mention of Alexander... not even the faintest awareness of the complete transformation that he was effecting.' Greece's division into independent, experimenting city-states made it a political laboratory whose lessons, Russell notes, became relevant again only much later, with the rise of the Italian cities in the Middle Ages, and remain relevant, in modified form, to debates about the proper size of a viable modern State.
philosophical_problems: Is the State a natural institution, prior in some sense to the individuals who compose it?
Is slavery ever natural and just, and if so, on what basis?
Is trade, and especially lending money at interest, a natural or an unnatural way of acquiring wealth?
What distinguishes good constitutions from bad ones, and is any one form of government simply best?
What causes political revolutions, and can they be prevented?
How large should a State be, and who should count as a citizen?

philosophers_discussed.name: Aristotle
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Primary subject: Russell reconstructs the Politics's account of the State's natural origin, slavery, trade and usury, critique of Plato's Republic, sixfold constitutional taxonomy, analysis of revolution and tyranny, and views on State size, citizenship, and education.

philosophers_discussed.name: Plato
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: His Republic is criticized at length by Aristotle (as reported by Russell) for giving the State too much unity, for the proposed abolition of the family, and for communism of property; Russell judges these to be among Aristotle's more persuasive arguments.

philosophers_discussed.name: Thales
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited in an anecdote: taunted for his poverty, he cornered the olive-press market to prove that philosophers could make money if they chose, though they think other things more important.

core_concepts.name: The State as natural and prior to the individual
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Aristotle argues that families combine into villages, villages into a self-sufficient State, and that although the State comes later in time, it is 'prior by nature' to the family and the individual, since a person (like a hand cut off from a body) cannot truly fulfil their purpose except as part of a State.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's organic conception of political community, in which the State, though the last stage in a natural sequence of family and village, is metaphysically prior to its parts because 'what each thing is when fully developed we call its nature,' and a part (like a severed hand) can be defined only by the function it performs within the functioning whole.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It grounds Aristotle's claim that 'the end of the State is the good life,' not mere economic exchange or crime prevention, and that 'he who founded the State was the greatest of benefactors,' since law and full human fulfilment depend on it.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Original to Aristotle's Politics, drawing on his biological conception of 'nature' as an organism's mature, functional end-state.
examples: 'A hand, when the body is destroyed, is... no longer a hand' -- illustrating that a part is defined by its function within a living whole.
'The State is the union of families and villages in a perfect and self-sufficing life... a happy and honourable life.'
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: The organic analogy for the State recurs throughout later political theory, both liberal and totalitarian.

core_concepts.name: Natural slavery
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Aristotle holds that some people are, by nature, suited only to be ruled and to do manual labor for others, and that enslaving such people is right, though he is uneasy about whether prisoners of war are always genuinely 'natural slaves.'
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's doctrine that certain individuals are naturally inferior in reason and thus fit only for subjection ('the man who is by nature not his own but another man's is by nature a slave'), that slavery of such persons is expedient and just, and that war waged against peoples who by nature ought to be ruled but refuse to submit is likewise just.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It shows Aristotle's Politics reflecting, rather than challenging, a central social institution of his time, and it supplied later thinkers with a philosophical vocabulary for justifying subjection on the basis of supposed natural inferiority.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Reflects the near-universal Greek assumption that slavery was a basic, unquestioned part of household and civic life.
examples: 'Slaves should not be Greeks, but of an inferior race with less spirit.'
objections: Russell notes the circularity Aristotle's own logic invites: since 'the only evidence as to nature's intentions must be derived from the outcome of war,' any victor can claim the vanquished were naturally meant to be ruled -- 'in every war... the victors are in the right and the vanquished in the wrong. Very satisfactory!'
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Provided a durable template for later justifications of conquest and subjection on grounds of supposed natural or racial inferiority.

core_concepts.name: Critique of trade and usury
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Aristotle distinguishes a thing's 'proper' use (wearing a shoe) from its 'improper' use (exchanging it for profit), and condemns money-lending at interest ('usury') as the most unnatural way of making money, since money is meant only to facilitate exchange, not to breed more money.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's economic doctrine (Politics I) that wealth acquired through household management of land is natural and has a proper limit, while wealth acquired through retail trade is unnatural and unlimited, with usury -- 'a gain out of money itself, and not from the natural object of it' -- condemned as the most unnatural mode of acquisition of all.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell traces this doctrine's long afterlife: it 'profoundly influenced scholastic casuistry' and shaped centuries of Christian and Islamic prohibition or regulation of interest-bearing loans, with the alignment of philosophical opinion tracking, Russell argues, the economic interests of whichever class -- landowners or, later, business creditors -- held philosophical influence at a given time.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Rooted in Aristotle's broader natural/unnatural distinction applied to economic activity.
examples: 'The most hated sort, and with the greatest reason, is usury, which makes a gain out of money itself, and not from the natural object of it.'
objections: Russell: 'the views of philosophers, with few exceptions, have coincided with the pecuniary interests of their class' -- Greek philosophers were landowners (hence anti-interest), medieval churchmen likewise held land (hence upheld the doctrine, reinforced by anti-Semitism against Jewish creditors), and only with the Reformation, when many earnest Protestants were business creditors, did Calvin and other Protestant divines begin sanctioning interest, with the Catholic Church eventually following suit.
competing_positions: The gradually triumphant Reformation-era view, sanctioned first by Calvin, that lending at interest is legitimate.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Shaped medieval scholastic economic doctrine for centuries; Russell directs readers to Tawney's Religion and the Rise of Capitalism for the fuller history, while noting Tawney's own account has 'a bias in favour of what is pre-capitalistic.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Medieval Christian condemnation of usury was reinforced by anti-Semitism, since much fluid capital was held by Jewish lenders.

core_concepts.name: Sixfold classification of constitutions
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Aristotle sorts governments into three good forms -- rule by one (monarchy), by the few best (aristocracy), or by the many for the common good (polity) -- and three corrupted counterparts -- tyranny, oligarchy, and democracy -- where rulers serve only their own interest; since 'the corruption of the best is worst,' tyranny is actually the worst of all six, making democracy, among bad governments, comparatively the best.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's taxonomy distinguishing governments by whether rulers pursue the common good (monarchy, aristocracy, polity) or their own narrow interest (tyranny, oligarchy, democracy respectively), further cross-cut by an economic criterion distinguishing oligarchy (rule by the rich, disregarding the poor) from democracy (rule by the poor/many, disregarding the rich).
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It gives Aristotle grounds for a qualified defense of democracy: because 'most actual governments are bad,' and the corruption of the best form (monarchy, corrupting into tyranny) is worse than the corruption of lesser forms, democracies, among the governments actually found in practice, tend to be the least bad.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Original systematization by Aristotle, drawing on his comparative survey of many actual Greek constitutions.
examples: Aristotle notes that in extreme Greek democracy, appointing magistrates by lot was considered democratic while electing them was considered oligarchic -- a use of 'democracy' more extreme than in modern usage.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: The good/corrupt pairing of constitutional forms became a standard framework in later Western political theory.

core_concepts.name: Causes of revolution and 'equality according to proportion'
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Aristotle argues that revolutions arise from the clash between democrats, who think that people equally free should be equal in everything, and oligarchs, who think that people superior in some respect deserve more of everything; he proposes preventing revolution through civic education, respect for law, and 'equality according to proportion' -- rewarding people in proportion to their merit.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's analysis (drawing on extensive comparative experience of Greek civil conflict) that revolution is chiefly caused by the competing partial justices of democratic and oligarchic factions, to be forestalled by government-aligned education, habitual respect for law even in small matters, and proportional (merit-based) rather than strictly equal distribution of political goods.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell uses it to expose a deep practical difficulty in Aristotle's own theory: since virtue is hard to measure and contested, 'proportionate justice' collapses in practice into measuring worth by income, undermining Aristotle's attempted distinction between a genuine aristocracy (rule of the virtuous) and a mere oligarchy (rule of the rich).
core_concepts.historical_origin: Drawn from Aristotle's wide comparative knowledge of Greek civil conflict, which Russell compares to 'formerly in Latin America' in frequency.
examples: An oligarchic oath quoted by Aristotle: 'I will be an enemy to the people, and will devise all the harm against them which I can.'
objections: Russell: virtue is difficult to measure and is 'a matter of party controversy'; in practice, 'virtue tends to be measured by income,' so the distinction Aristotle wants between aristocracy and oligarchy 'is only possible where there is a very well-established hereditary nobility,' and even then breaks down once a large non-noble rich class arises and must be admitted to power to avert revolution.
competing_positions: Russell's own conclusion that 'all social inequality, in the long run, is inequality of income,' which he treats as part of the argument for democracy over any scheme of 'proportionate justice' based on supposedly measurable merit.

core_concepts.name: The anatomy of tyranny
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Aristotle gives an almost step-by-step manual for how a tyrant keeps power: eliminate anyone of outstanding merit, ban clubs, common meals, and education that might breed solidarity, keep subjects isolated and impoverished, use spies (including women and slaves as informers), and keep the people occupied and dependent through great public works or war.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's description, in an 'ironically Machiavellian tone,' of the practical techniques by which a tyrant retains power: suppressing potential rivals, prohibiting associations and education likely to foster hostile solidarity, maintaining surveillance through informers, sowing internal discord, impoverishing subjects, and engaging in constant public works or war to keep the population occupied and dependent on a leader.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell calls this 'the one [passage], of the whole book, most appropriate to the present day' -- writing during the Second World War -- treating it as an uncanny anticipation of twentieth-century totalitarian technique, despite its twenty-three-century age.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Drawn from Aristotle's observation of actual historical tyrannies across the Greek world.
examples: The tyrant 'should employ spies, like the female detectives at Syracuse.'
He should 'make war, in order that his subjects may have something to do and be always in want of a leader.'
competing_positions: Aristotle notes an alternative, less brutal method of preserving tyranny, through moderation and outward piety, without deciding which method is more likely to succeed.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Anticipates, per Russell, techniques associated with twentieth-century fascist and totalitarian regimes.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: The alternative, gentler survival strategy Aristotle mentions involves the tyrant 'seeming religious.'

arguments.title: The organism argument for the State's priority
premises: A thing's nature is what it is when fully developed.
A part (such as a hand) can perform its function only as part of a living whole; severed from the whole, it is no longer truly what it was.
The individual human being can fulfil their purpose only as part of a State.
arguments.conclusion: The State, though later in time than the family and the individual, is prior to them 'by nature,' since the whole is prior to the part.
arguments.explanation: Russell presents this as Aristotle's foundational argument for treating political community as natural rather than merely conventional, directly opposing any purely contractual or instrumental view of the State.
implications: Grounds Aristotle's claim that the State's purpose is 'the good life,' not merely security or economic exchange, and that founding a State is the greatest possible benefaction to humanity.

arguments.title: Aristotle's argument against usury
premises: Every thing has a proper (natural) use and may also be put to an improper (unnatural) use.
Money's proper use is as a medium of exchange, not as a thing that itself generates more of itself.
Usury makes a gain 'out of money itself,' not from the natural object for which money exists.
arguments.conclusion: Usury is 'of all modes of getting wealth... the most unnatural,' and justly hated.
arguments.explanation: This argument, Russell notes, 'profoundly influenced scholastic casuistry' and helped shape centuries of prohibition or suspicion of interest-bearing lending in medieval Christian (and later Islamic) economic thought.
objections: Russell's historical-sociological rebuttal: opinion on usury has tracked class interest throughout history -- landowning classes (ancient Greek philosophers, medieval churchmen) opposed interest, while commercial creditor classes (Reformation-era Protestant businessmen) eventually secured its acceptance -- suggesting the 'natural/unnatural' framing rationalized, rather than derived, the economically convenient position of whichever class held philosophical influence.
implications: Its long afterlife illustrates, for Russell, a general pattern: philosophical arguments about economic morality tend to track the economic interests of the class producing them.

arguments.title: Aristotle's critique of Plato's communism of the family
premises: What is common to the greatest number of people receives the least care.
Under Plato's scheme, calling many young people 'sons' makes them common to many 'fathers.'
arguments.conclusion: Plato's proposed abolition of the private family would not extend paternal-style affection to all, as Plato hoped, but would instead dilute it to nothing -- 'it is better to be a cousin in reality than a "son" in Plato's sense,' and 'Plato's plan would make love watery.'
arguments.explanation: Russell finds this among Aristotle's more persuasive criticisms of the Republic, alongside the related worry that abolishing private property removes the very possibility of virtues like generosity and benevolence, which require something private to give away.
implications: Supports Aristotle's alternative proposal: private property retained, but citizens trained in benevolence so that its use is 'largely common' -- a compromise Russell notes Aristotle himself does not fully develop into a workable scheme.

arguments.title: The 'corruption of the best is worst' argument for a qualified defense of democracy
premises: Monarchy is better than aristocracy, and aristocracy is better than polity, among the good constitutions.
The corruption of the best form of government is the worst corrupted form.
Tyranny is the corruption of monarchy, oligarchy of aristocracy, and democracy of polity.
arguments.conclusion: Tyranny is worse than oligarchy, and oligarchy is worse than democracy; therefore, since most actual governments are bad ones, democracies tend, among real-world governments, to be comparatively the best.
arguments.explanation: Russell highlights this as an unexpected result of Aristotle's otherwise hierarchical ranking of constitutions: theoretical preference for monarchy or aristocracy does not translate into a preference for their practical, real-world substitutes, since those forms corrupt into the worst outcomes.
implications: Yields Aristotle's 'qualified defence of democracy,' distinguishing his theoretical constitutional ranking from his comparative judgment of actually existing governments.

key_distinctions: Proper use of a thing (e.g., wearing a shoe) vs. improper/exchange use (selling it)
Natural wealth-getting (household management of land, which has a natural limit) vs. unnatural wealth-getting (trade and especially usury, which has none)
Good constitutions (monarchy, aristocracy, polity, ruling for the common good) vs. their corrupt counterparts (tyranny, oligarchy, democracy, ruling for the rulers' own interest)
Oligarchy (economic rule by the rich, disregarding the poor) vs. democracy (economic rule by the poor/many, disregarding the rich)
Aristocracy (rule of the genuinely virtuous) vs. oligarchy (rule of the merely rich) -- a distinction Russell argues collapses in practice
Citizens (who alone may hold political power and receive full education) vs. laborers, tradesmen, and husbandmen (excluded from citizenship as 'ignoble and inimical to virtue')
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: The bulk of the chapter is structured around Aristotle's direct, sustained critique of Plato's Republic (previous relevant chapters), targeting its excessive unity, abolition of private family, and communism of property; Russell notes that, on balance, 'if anything could make me' agree with Plato's communism, 'it would be Aristotle's arguments against him' -- a wry indication that Russell finds Aristotle's critique less than fully persuasive even while reporting it.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell traces the usury doctrine's long afterlife through medieval scholastic casuistry into the Reformation (Calvin's sanctioning of interest) and directs readers to Tawney's Religion and the Rise of Capitalism. He also draws an extended, explicit parallel between Aristotle's account of how a tyrant retains power and the practices of contemporary (1941) totalitarian dictatorship, and compares Aristotle's problem of adequate State size to the modern problem of national self-sufficiency and defense, concluding that 'nothing smaller than America and the British Empire combined' would satisfy Aristotle's own logic in the twentieth century.
political_social_context: Russell situates the Politics within the world of the Greek City State exactly as it was ending: Aristotle wrote at the very moment Macedonian power was making the City State obsolete, yet the book shows no awareness of this. Russell also traces a long historical arc from Aristotle's ideal of government by 'cultured gentlemen' (realized, at its height, in Periclean Athens) through the Renaissance and eighteenth century, to its erosion by the French Revolution's democracy, industrialism, and popular education -- concluding that 'both for good and evil... the day of the cultured gentleman is past.'
religion_science_culture_context: Aristotle's discussion of usury, filtered through medieval Christian scholasticism, became entangled with anti-Semitism, since Jewish lenders held much of the available fluid capital that Christian landowners and clergy needed but were forbidden by doctrine to supply themselves.
russell_presentation: Russell moves through the Politics roughly in its own order: a scatter of vivid anecdotes (Euripides and Decamnichus, marriage-age rules, Thales and the olive presses) as light relief before 'more serious matters'; the argument that the State is natural and prior to the individual; the extended discussion of slavery, including Aristotle's own uneasy qualifications about whether conquered peoples are truly 'natural slaves'; the critique of trade and, at length, of usury; Aristotle's critique of Plato's Republic (unity, family, communism); the sixfold classification of constitutions and its resulting qualified defense of democracy; the analysis of the causes of revolution and Aristotle's proposed remedies; the extended, almost manual-like account of how a tyrant retains power; the discussion of ideal State size (with Russell noting Aristotle's own apparent inconsistency about self-sufficiency versus trade); the restriction of citizenship away from laborers and tradesmen; and the unfinished discussion of education for citizens, aimed at cultured leisure rather than utility. Russell closes with his own broader historical reflection on the rise and fall of the ideal of the 'cultured gentleman' that Aristotle's Politics assumes throughout.
critical_context: Russell repeatedly intervenes with pointed, often ironic criticism rather than neutral summary: he calls Aristotle's logic on the justice of enslaving conquered peoples 'very satisfactory!' precisely because it lets every victor claim justification; he supplies an extensive Layer-3 sociological account (via Tawney) of how philosophical opinion on usury has tracked the economic interests of whichever class held influence; he flags the practical collapse of 'proportionate justice' into rule-by-wealth; and he explicitly reads the chapter's account of tyranny's survival techniques against the fascist dictatorships of his own day (the chapter includes Russell's own dated aside, 'This was written in May, 1941'). He closes with an extended historical argument of his own -- tracing the rise and fall of government by 'cultured gentlemen' from Periclean Athens through the Renaissance to its dissolution by democracy, industrialism, and popular education -- that goes well beyond anything explicit in Aristotle's text.
key_takeaways: Aristotle argues the State is natural and, in a functional sense, prior to the individual and the family, existing for 'the good life' rather than mere security or exchange.

Aristotle defends natural slavery in principle, but Russell notes the argument's circularity: since only the outcome of war reveals who was 'meant' to be ruled, any conqueror can justify any conquest.

Aristotle condemns usury as the most unnatural mode of wealth-getting; Russell traces how philosophical opinion on interest tracked the economic interests of landowning versus creditor classes across history.

Aristotle's sixfold classification (monarchy/aristocracy/polity vs. tyranny/oligarchy/democracy) yields, via the principle that 'the corruption of the best is worst,' a qualified practical defense of democracy among actually existing governments.

Aristotle's near-manual description of how tyrants retain power (isolating subjects, banning associations, using spies, sowing discord, waging war) struck Russell, writing in 1941, as strikingly applicable to contemporary totalitarian dictatorship.

Aristotle restricts citizenship to those with leisure, excluding laborers and tradesmen, and envisions education aimed at producing 'cultured gentlemen' -- an ideal Russell traces down to its eventual dissolution by democracy, industrialism, and mass education.
study_notes:
This is one of the chapter's most argument-dense entries, so it helps to track Aristotle's recurring analytical move: for almost every institution he discusses (the State, slavery, trade, constitutions, revolution, tyranny), he first asks what its natural or proper function is, and then evaluates actual or proposed practice against that standard. Once you see this pattern, the chapter's structure becomes much more predictable -- 'proper use' and 'improper use,' 'natural' and 'unnatural,' 'good' constitutions and their 'corrupt' counterparts are all instances of the same underlying method.

Pay close attention to where Russell steps outside pure summary to offer his own historical or sociological analysis, since these are the passages doing the heaviest interpretive work: the extended discussion of usury and class interest, the deflation of 'proportionate justice' into rule-by-wealth, and the closing historical sweep from Periclean Athens to the twentieth century. These sections model a recurring Russellian technique -- testing an ancient philosophical claim against its real economic and political consequences over the following centuries, rather than assessing it only as an abstract argument.

The tyranny passage deserves special attention as the chapter's emotional high point: Russell explicitly dates his own commentary ('written in May, 1941') to underline how directly Aristotle's twenty-three-century-old analysis seemed to describe contemporary fascism. Read this section as an example of how a historian of philosophy can use an ancient text to illuminate present events without claiming the ancient author foresaw them.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Aristotle's claim that some people are naturally suited only to be ruled by others and can rightly be enslaved.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Aristotle's doctrine that certain individuals, naturally deficient in reason, are fit only for subjection, making their enslavement expedient and just, extended (controversially) to justify war against peoples deemed naturally fit to be ruled.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Lending money at interest, which Aristotle condemned as the most unnatural way to make money.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: In Aristotle's usage, any lending of money at interest (not only exorbitant rates, as in later usage), condemned as unnatural because it generates a gain from money itself rather than from money's proper function as a medium of exchange.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Aristotle's term for the good version of rule by the many, aimed at the common good rather than narrow self-interest.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The good, non-corrupted form of rule by the many in Aristotle's sixfold constitutional taxonomy, retaining, per Aristotle, some oligarchic elements and distinguished from democracy chiefly by aiming at the common good.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that people should be treated unequally in proportion to their merit, rather than given strictly equal shares.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Aristotle's proposed remedy for revolution, distributing political goods in proportion to virtue rather than by strict equality; Russell argues this collapses in practice into distribution by wealth, since virtue is not reliably measurable.
related_concepts: Causes of revolution and 'equality according to proportion'

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Aristotle's assumed ideal citizen: a person of leisure who combines aristocratic manners with a love of learning and the arts.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The implicit aim of Aristotle's educational and citizenship proposals -- production of a leisured class combining aristocratic mentality with cultivated taste -- which Russell traces historically from Periclean Athens through the Renaissance to its dissolution by modern democracy, industrialism, and popular education.
related_concepts: The State as natural and prior to the individual

questions.prompt: According to Aristotle, why is the State 'prior by nature' to the family and the individual, even though it comes later in time?
questions.answer: Because a thing's nature is what it is when fully developed, and a part (like a severed hand) can only truly fulfil its function as part of a living whole; individuals can likewise only fulfil their purpose as part of a State.
questions.explanation: This organism analogy grounds Aristotle's claim that the State exists for 'the good life,' not mere exchange or security.

questions.prompt: What objection does Russell raise to Aristotle's justification of enslaving conquered peoples as 'natural slaves'?
questions.answer: Since the only evidence of who is naturally meant to be ruled is the outcome of war, and no nation will admit it was meant to be governed, any victor can claim justification -- making the argument circular and, in Russell's words, letting 'the victors' always be 'in the right and the vanquished... in the wrong.'
questions.explanation: Russell calls this consequence 'very satisfactory!' with evident irony.

questions.prompt: Why does Aristotle condemn usury as the most unnatural way of acquiring wealth?
questions.answer: Because money's proper function is as a medium of exchange, and usury makes a gain 'out of money itself,' not from money's natural object.
questions.explanation: Russell traces this doctrine's long, class-interest-inflected afterlife through medieval and Reformation economic thought.

questions.prompt: Compare Aristotle's sixfold classification of constitutions with his ultimate, qualified defense of democracy. How does the second follow from the first?
questions.answer: Aristotle ranks monarchy, aristocracy, and polity as good, and tyranny, oligarchy, and democracy as their corrupted counterparts; but since the corruption of the best form is the worst, tyranny is worse than oligarchy, which is worse than democracy -- so, since most actual governments are bad, democracies tend to be the least bad among real-world governments.
questions.explanation: This is Aristotle's 'corruption of the best is worst' argument.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Aristotle's argument against Plato's proposed abolition of the private family in the Republic.
questions.answer: What is common to the greatest number receives the least care; under Plato's scheme, calling many young people 'sons' makes them common to many 'fathers'; therefore the scheme would not extend paternal affection to everyone but would instead dilute it to nothing -- 'Plato's plan would make love watery.'
questions.explanation: Russell finds this among Aristotle's more persuasive criticisms of Plato.

questions.prompt: List three techniques Aristotle describes for how a tyrant retains power, and explain why Russell finds this passage especially significant.
questions.answer: Examples include eliminating people of outstanding merit, banning clubs and education likely to breed solidarity, using spies and informers, sowing quarrels, impoverishing subjects, and waging war to keep them occupied; Russell calls this 'the one [passage], of the whole book, most appropriate to the present day,' writing during the Second World War.
questions.explanation: Russell explicitly dates his commentary to May 1941.

questions.prompt: What inconsistency does Russell note in Aristotle's discussion of the ideal size of a State?
questions.answer: Aristotle says the State should be self-sufficient, small enough to be surveyed from a hilltop, yet also says it should have export and import trade -- which Russell flags as 'an inconsistency.'
questions.explanation: Russell extends this discussion into a reflection on modern national self-sufficiency and defense.

flashcards.front: According to Aristotle, what is the end (purpose) of the State?
flashcards.back: 'The good life' -- a happy and honourable existence, not merely economic exchange or the prevention of crime.

flashcards.front: How does Aristotle's organism analogy (the severed hand) support his view of the State?
flashcards.back: A part can only fulfil its function within a living whole, just as an individual can only fulfil their purpose as part of a State -- making the State prior 'by nature' to the individual.

flashcards.front: What is Russell's objection to Aristotle's justification for enslaving conquered peoples?
flashcards.back: Only the outcome of war reveals who was naturally meant to be ruled, so any victor can claim justification -- an argument that, Russell notes ironically, always favors the victors.

flashcards.front: Why does Aristotle call usury the most unnatural way of acquiring wealth?
flashcards.back: Because it produces a gain from money itself rather than from money's proper function as a medium of exchange.

flashcards.front: What historical pattern does Russell trace regarding philosophical views on usury/interest?
flashcards.back: Opinion tracked class interest: landowning classes (ancient Greek philosophers, medieval clergy) opposed interest, while creditor/business classes (Reformation Protestants) eventually secured its acceptance.

flashcards.front: What is Aristotle's chief objection to Plato's proposed abolition of the private family?
flashcards.back: What is common to many is cared for by none; extending 'son' to all dilutes rather than extends paternal affection -- 'Plato's plan would make love watery.'

flashcards.front: What are the three good and three corrupt forms of government in Aristotle's classification?
flashcards.back: Good: monarchy, aristocracy, polity. Corrupt: tyranny, oligarchy, democracy.

flashcards.front: How does Aristotle's 'corruption of the best is worst' principle lead to a qualified defense of democracy?
flashcards.back: Since tyranny (corrupted monarchy) is worse than oligarchy, which is worse than democracy, and most actual governments are bad, democracies tend to be the least bad governments in practice.

flashcards.front: What does Russell say is the practical problem with Aristotle's 'equality according to proportion'?
flashcards.back: Virtue is hard to measure and contested, so in practice proportionate justice collapses into measuring worth by wealth/income.

flashcards.front: Name three techniques Aristotle describes for how a tyrant retains power.
flashcards.back: Eliminating people of outstanding merit, banning clubs/education that build solidarity, using spies and informers, sowing internal quarrels, impoverishing subjects, and waging war to keep people occupied.

flashcards.front: Why does Russell call Aristotle's tyranny passage 'most appropriate to the present day'?
flashcards.back: Because, writing in 1941, Russell saw it as an uncanny anticipation of contemporary fascist/totalitarian technique.

flashcards.front: Who is excluded from citizenship in Aristotle's ideal State?
flashcards.back: Laborers, tradesmen ('mechanics'), and husbandmen, since such lives are deemed 'ignoble and inimical to virtue' and incompatible with the leisure citizenship requires.

flashcards.front: What historical arc does Russell trace regarding the ideal of the 'cultured gentleman' that underlies Aristotle's Politics?
flashcards.back: From its height in Periclean Athens, through the Renaissance and eighteenth century, to its dissolution by the French Revolution's democracy, industrialism, and popular education.

quiz.explanation: Usury generates gain from money itself rather than money's proper use as a medium of exchange.

quiz.prompt: Aristotle's sixfold classification pairs monarchy with its corrupt form, ___.
quiz.explanation: Tyranny is the corrupted form of monarchy.

quiz.prompt: Why does Aristotle's logic lead to a qualified defense of democracy among actually existing governments?
options: Because democracy is always the theoretically best constitution
Because the corruption of the best form (monarchy -> tyranny) is worst, making democracy the least bad of the actually common bad governments
Because Aristotle personally preferred rule by the poor
quiz.explanation: Tyranny is worse than oligarchy, which is worse than democracy, so among bad (actual) governments democracy tends to be least bad.

quiz.prompt: Russell argues that Aristotle's 'equality according to proportion' works well in practice because virtue is easy to measure.
quiz.explanation: Russell argues virtue is hard to measure and contested, so proportionate justice collapses in practice into rule by wealth.
quiz.related_concept: Causes of revolution and 'equality according to proportion'

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is NOT among the tyrant-preservation techniques Aristotle describes?
options: Banning clubs and education that foster solidarity
Distributing land equally among all citizens
quiz.explanation: Equal land distribution is not among Aristotle's listed techniques; the others are explicitly described.

quiz.prompt: Match each critique to its target: (1) 'Plato's plan would make love watery', (2) 'Very satisfactory!' (ironic), (3) tracks class interest across history.
options: (1) Aristotle's critique of Plato's abolition of the family; (2) Russell's critique of Aristotle's natural-slavery/war argument; (3) Russell's critique of the usury doctrine's history
(1) Russell's critique of Aristotle's Politics as a whole; (2) Aristotle's critique of Plato; (3) Aristotle's critique of democracy
All three target Aristotle's theory of tyranny
(1) targets usury; (2) targets slavery; (3) targets Plato's communism
quiz.explanation: Each quotation/critique targets a distinct argument discussed in the chapter.

quiz.prompt: Aristotle includes laborers and tradesmen among the citizens who should hold political power in his ideal State.
quiz.explanation: Aristotle excludes laborers and tradesmen from citizenship as 'ignoble and inimical to virtue.'
quiz.related_concept: The State as natural and prior to the individual

quiz.prompt: What inconsistency does Russell identify in Aristotle's discussion of ideal State size?
options: Aristotle says States should be enormous and also tiny
Aristotle says the State should be self-sufficient yet also says it should have export and import trade
Aristotle contradicts himself about whether States need citizens at all
quiz.explanation: Russell explicitly flags this as 'an inconsistency' in Aristotle's text.
quiz.related_concept: The State as natural and prior to the individual
